claims.statement: WebDecoy separates one-off self-hosted captcha verification from later-request client-signal enforcement: the captcha service can issue a token after scoring browser evidence and proof of work, while `clientSignals()` reads a server-recorded session verdict to deny or throttle a subsequent request.

Browser signals are probabilistic client-controlled evidence rather than proof of humanity; `ClientSignalRule` deliberately returns allowed `NOT_RUN` results when the request has no browser session or no recorded verdict.

The client exposes checkbox, invisible, and one-shot browser flows: checkbox rendering uses `CaptchaWidget`, `invisible()` creates an `InvisibleSession`, and `execute()` creates a temporary invisible session with auto-scoring disabled then destroys it.

An `InvisibleSession` collects behavioral, environmental, temporal, form, sensor, and metadata evidence, waits for its configured minimum collection time, hashes the serialized signal object, solves PoW bound to that hash, and posts the signals, hash, solution, and timing to `/score`.

With `autoScore` enabled, `InvisibleSession` synchronously intercepts form submission when its score is absent or older than 60 seconds, injects `webdecoy_token`, resubmits after a successful score, dispatches a blocked event for an unsuccessful score, and fail-opens by submitting if scoring throws.

The client PoW solver fetches a server challenge when configured and uses inline Web Workers that scan disjoint nonce strides; absent or failed server access falls back to a locally generated challenge.

`createCaptchaEndpoints()` is the framework-neutral endpoint surface under configurable `/__webdecoy` by default: it handles challenge issuance, checkbox verification, invisible scoring, and token verification, returning `null` for non-captcha paths.

The Express, Fastify, and Next.js integrations delegate captcha semantics to `createCaptchaEndpoints()`; Express requires JSON parsing ahead of its middleware, while the adapters resolve the IP they pass to the endpoint service.

Server challenges are HMAC-signed, expire after five minutes, use leading-zero SHA-256 difficulty that defaults to 4 and scales up for datacenter IPs or challenge-request rate, and are consumed after a valid solution to prevent replay.

`Captcha.verify()` checks an optional raw-signals commitment, verifies PoW, feeds its outcome and request context to `DetectionEngine`, and issues a token only for a successful verdict; `score()` uses that same pipeline and adds the caller action.
Detection scoring is an in-process aggregation of PoW, automation and browser evidence; default recommendations are `allow` below 0.3, `challenge` below 0.6, and `block` at 0.6 or higher.

A captcha token is base64url JSON signed with HMAC, contains site key, timestamp, score, and an IP hash, expires in five minutes, and verification enforces signature, optional IP match, and single-use replay protection.
Production requires a nonempty non-default captcha signing secret; the development fallback is rejected when `NODE_ENV` is production.

When `signalStore` and a top-level score-body `sessionId` are provided, `/score` stores the score and recommendation keyed by that ID and echoes the ID; it otherwise returns a score without persisting a verdict.

`ClientSignalRule` reads `wd_cs` from the cookie before `x-wd-session`, applies the stored `block` recommendation unless `minScore` overrides it, supports `DENY` or `THROTTLE`, and makes a matching bad result observational when `dryRun` is true.

`ClientSignalStore` supports sync and async backends; for async backends the rule prefetches the verdict in `prepare()`, while `MemoryClientSignalStore` defaults to a 15-minute TTL, maximum 10,000 entries, expiry-on-read, and oldest-entry eviction.

The currently inspected stock `InvisibleSession` does not complete the score-to-rule session handoff: it places its generated ID in `signals.meta.sessionId` but does not send the top-level `sessionId` consumed by `/score`, and it does not set the `wd_cs` cookie.

The built-in challenge, token, detection, rate, and client-signal stores are in-process defaults; multi-instance deployments must replace them with shared implementations, including atomic replay-consumption behavior for challenges and tokens.

Focused tests cover secret validation, PoW and token replay/expiry/IP binding, end-to-end captcha verification, normalized HTTP routing, and client-signal store and enforcement behavior; the monorepo test command is `npm test`.
